Today


Introduction to multiple regression

Motivation
Interpretation of coefs

Assumptions of multiple regression
Effect size and power
Plotting
Write-up




Roadmap. Motivation. See MR in action.
Q: I said that MR is an extension of LR, which allows us to consider more than 1 vars. But have you already considered more than 1 variable before? A: YES! with ANOVA. But why is that different? Hybrid is also called ancova
We’ll build on simple regression — add more predictors
Then tackle the messiness: assumptions, outliers, multicollinearity
End with how to report results properly

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Simple Linear Model







SLR: One predictor, one outcome
X predicts Y — that’s our foundation
Single arrow, single relationship

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Multiple predictors in linear regression







Now we add more Xs
Multiple arrows pointing to Y
Same logic, just more of it

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Multiple regression
\[\begin{align}
\hat{Y} &= b_0 + \beta_1 X
\end{align}\]
\[\large \hat{Y} = b_0 + b_1X_1 + b_2X_2 + \dots+b_kX_k\]

Simple as adding predictors to our linear equation



Simple regression on top, multiple regression below
We just keep adding terms
Q: what do you anctipate to change in the outputs?

– A: Each X gets its own slope

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Multiple regression equation

\[\large \hat{Y} = b_0 + b_1X_1 + b_2X_2 + \dots+b_kX_k\]

\(\hat{Y}\) = predicted value on the outcome variable Y
\(b_0\) = predicted value on Y when all Xs = 0
\(X_k\) = predictor variables
\(b_k\) = unstandardized regression coefficients
\(k\) = the number of predictor variables




Let’s break this apart
Y-hat is our prediction
b₀ is the intercept — Y when all predictors are zero (just like SLR)
Each b is a slope, each X is a predictor
k is how many predictors we have

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Straight Line to Hyperplane



More than two predictors (plane)

Multi-dimensional space

Regression coefficients are “partial” regression coefficients

Slope for variable X1 (\(b_1\)) predicts the change in Y per unit X1 holding X2 constant
Slope for variable X2 (\(b_2\)) predicts the change in Y per unit X2 holding X1 constant














With one predictor we had a line that was fit to the data
With Two predictors we are fitting a plane
More than two: terminology is a hyperplane (hard to visualize)
Key insight: each coefficient is now “partial” – It tells you the effect of X₁ after controlling for X₂ – what does that mean? It means, you stay at a fixed point in X1, then X2 has a slope – 2 different slopes => 2 coefficients

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Individual Predictors


We test the individual predictors with a t-test:

\(t = \frac{b}{SE}\)
Therefore, the model for each individual predictor is our coefficient b
Single sample t-test to determine if the b value is different from zero





How do we test if each predictor matters?
Same t-test logic
Take the coefficient, divide by its standard error
(Many of these tests are SNR / proportion of variance explained)
Is b different from zero? That’s our question for each predictor

title: Multiple Regression
text:
More predictors => more problems

Assumptions

Linearity
Independence
Normality of residuals
Equal error (“homoskedasticity”)




Issues:

Missingness
Factors are correlated with one another (multicollinearity)
Unusual values/outliers





More predictors = more things can go wrong
Standard assumptions still apply: linearity, independence, normality, homoskedasticity
New issues: missing data, multicollinearity, outliers
Let’s tackle each

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Problems

Missingness

list-wise deletion (removes entire row where missingness occurs)



nomiss <- master %>%
  drop_na() # drop missing data

#base r
nomiss <- master %>%
  na.omit() 

nrow(master)

[1] 267

nrow(nomiss)

[1] 266




Missing data? R uses listwise deletion by default
One missing value in a row? Whole row gone
We went from 267 to 266 — not bad here
Can be catastrophic with more missingness
Later in the semester, we’ll look at other solutions

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Problems


Multicolinearity

You want X and Y to be correlated
You do not want the Xs to be highly correlated










We want X and Y correlated
We don’t want the Xs correlated with each other
Figure: We want as much of the red circle to be calculated!
Next: we also want blues to be seperated! If predictors overlap too much, we can’t untangle their unique effects!! which variable to give credit to! It’s also redundancy.

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Multicolinearity


Problems

Extreme cases (complete collinearity) = Nonidentifiable model
“Unstable” regression coefficients (“bouncing betas”)

Imprecise estimation

Large standard errors

Increased Type II errors

Not detecting a difference when there is one







Extreme case: predictors perfectly correlated — model can’t be estimated at all
Less extreme: “bouncing betas” — coefficients become unstable
Standard errors inflate
You miss real effects (Type II errors)

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Multicolinearity

Tolerance

Measures influence of one predictor on another
If predictors are highly correlated, tolerance gets smaller


\[Tolerance=1- R^2_j\]

where \(R^2_j\) is the proportion of variation in X that is explained by the linear combination of the other predictors in the model



Tolerance: how much variance in X₁ is NOT explained by other Xs
Formula: 1 - R²
Lower tolerance = more problematic
The predictor is redundant with others
“How much unique information do I have about X1?”

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Multicolinearity

VIF (variance inflation factor)

How much does our estimates (SEs) change due to the correlation


\[VIF=\frac{1}{1- R^2_j}\]

Rule of thumb:

VIF > 10 indicates issues




VIF is the inverse of tolerance
“How much damage is being done?”
How much are standard errors inflated due to collinearity?
Rule of thumb: VIF > 10 is trouble, some say > 5

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Multicolinearity

Check multicolinearity in your data


#easystats performance package
#plot(check_collinearity(model_fit))



Easy to check with check_collinearity()
Our predictors look fine — low VIF values
No multicollinearity concerns here

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Multicolinearity


Strategies

Anticipate collinearity issues at the design stage
Depends: Drop variable if there’s no theoretical pay-off anyway
Depends: Fit separate models and compare fit
Depends: Increase sample size
Depends: Orthogonalize predictors experimentally
Depends: Use alternative approaches, such as ridge regression or LASSO
Do not do anything about it (if prediction is your goal)





What if you have multicollinearity?
Options depend on your goal
Drop redundant predictors, combine them into composites
Use regularization (ridge, LASSO)
Increase sample size
Or — if predicting is all you care about — ignore it
Predictions stay fine; it’s the individual coefficients that suffer

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Identifying unusual cases







Outliers matter more in regression
One weird point can drag the whole line
We need systematic ways to find them

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Influential points

An observation or case is influential if removing it substantially changes the coefficients of the regression model


Influence = Leverage x Distance (outliers)








Key formula: Influence = Leverage × Distance
Leverage: how extreme is the X value?
Distance: how far is Y from the prediction?
Both matter — high leverage + large residual = influential point

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Influential points


Influential points have a large impact on the coefficients and standard errors used for inference

Can be on x or y variables

These points can sometimes be identified in a scatterplot if there is only one predictor variable

This is often not the case when there are multiple predictors

We will use measures to quantify an individual observation’s influence on the regression model

Leverage, Standardized residuals , and Cook’s distance





These points mess with your coefficients and standard errors
With one predictor, you might spot them in a scatterplot
Multiple predictors? Need diagnostic measures
Three key measures: leverage, standardized residuals, Cook’s distance

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Leverage

Deals with Xs


Measure of geometric distance of the observation’s predictor point (\(X_{i1}\), \(X_{i2}\)) from center point of the predictor space

\[
h_i = \dfrac{1}{n} + \dfrac{\left(x_i -\overline{x}\right)^2}{\sum_{j=1}^{n}{\left(x_j -\overline{x}\right)^2}} \qquad \text{and}\qquad \overline{h} = \dfrac{k}{n}  \qquad \text{and}\qquad \dfrac{1}{n} \leq h_i \leq 1.0
\]






Note



In multiple regression \(h_i\) measures distance from the centroid (point of means) of Xs




Leverage (h): how unusual is this observation’s X values?
Far from the center of predictor space = high leverage
Points on the edge of the X distribution have more “pull” on the regression line

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Leverage







Visual representation
Points far from the center have high leverage
They have more influence on where the line goes
Not necessarily bad — but watch them

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Leverage

We say a point is high leverage if:

\[
h_i > \frac{2K+2}{N}
\]

K is the number of predictors
N is the sample size


k <- 3 ##number of IVs/predictors
# label 1 if out 0 if not
model_out<- model_fit  %>%
  augment() %>%
  mutate(lev_out = ifelse(.hat>(2*+2)/nrow(.),1, 0))

model_out

Threshold formula: h > (2k+2)/n
k predictors, n observations
The .hat column from augment() gives you leverage values
Compare to the threshold, flag the high ones
for each data point

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Standardized Residuals

Distance

how far away y point is from line


\[
std.res_i = \frac{y_i - \hat{y}_i}{\hat{\sigma}_\epsilon\sqrt{1-h_i}}
\]

Where \(\hat{\sigma}_\epsilon\) is regression standard error


Use cut-off > 3



Now the Y side
How far is each point from the line?
Standardized residuals account for leverage too
Rule: |standardized residual| > 3 is suspicious

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Standardized Residuals

# label 1 if out 0 if not
model_out<- model_fit  %>%
  augment() %>%
  mutate(lev_out = ifelse(.hat>(2*k+2)/nrow(.),1, 0), 
         std_out=ifelse(abs(.std.resid) > 3, 1, 0))


library(olsrr)

ols_plot_resid_stand(model_fit)










Visual inspection
Most residuals cluster near zero
Outliers stick out
The olsrr package makes nice plots

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Leverage and Distance



Montoya




Four quadrants to think about
Low leverage + small residual: typical points (good)
This is what we want most of our data to look like

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Leverage and distance



Montoya




High leverage + small residual: unusual X but fits the pattern
Low leverage + large residual: unusual Y but not very influential
These are less concerning

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Leverage and distance



Montoya




High leverage + large residual: TROUBLE
These are your influential points
They can dramatically change your regression line

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Cook’s distance

Influence (Cook’s Distance)

A measure of how much of an effect that single case has on the whole model

How close it lies to general line (residuals)
It’s leverage \[
D_i = \frac{(std.res_i)^2}{k + 1}\bigg(\frac{h_i}{1-h_i}\bigg)
\]
Threshold:



\[
\frac{4}{N-K-1}
\]


Cook’s D combines everything
How much would coefficients change if we removed this point?
Formula incorporates both leverage and residuals
Threshold: 4/(n-k-1)

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Cook’s distance

# label 1 if out 0 if not
model_out<- model_fit  %>%
  augment() %>%
  mutate(lev_out = ifelse(.hat>(2*k+2)/nrow(.),1, 0),
         std_out=ifelse(abs(.std.resid) > 3, 1, 0), 
         cook_out = ifelse(.cooksd > (4 / (nrow(.) - 3 - 1)), 1, 0))


library(olsrr)
ols_plot_cooksd_bar(model_fit)










Bar plot of Cook’s D
Tall bars = influential points
Easy to spot
Red line is threshold

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Combine Metrics

What do I do with all these numbers?

Create a total score for the number of indicators a data point has
You can decide what rule to use, but a suggestion is 2 or more indicators is an outliers



# label 1 if out 0 if not
model_out<- model_fit  %>%
  augment() %>%
  mutate(lev_out = ifelse(.hat>(2*k+2)/nrow(.),1, 0), cook_out = ifelse(.cooksd > (4 / (nrow(.) - 3 - 1)), 1, 0), std_out=ifelse(.std.resid >= 3, 1, 0)) %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(sum_out=lev_out+cook_out+std_out) %>%
  filter(sum_out < 2)


nrow(nomiss)

[1] 266

nrow(model_out)

[1] 255




Multiple indicators, multiple decisions
My suggestion: flag points that exceed 2+ thresholds
More robust than any single measure
Create a sum score, filter out the problems

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Easystats: Check_outliers

Use consensus method

If half of methods say point is outlier, get rid of it



# will estimate all outliers methods
outliers_list <- check_outliers(model_fit, method = "all")

# provides a col called outliers with prob of outliers by method (50% more than half said ob was outlier)

out_data <-insight::get_data(model_fit)[outliers_list, ] # Show outliers data

# get rid of values in outliers list in the main dataset 
clean_data <- anti_join(nomiss,out_data, by=c("CESD_total", "PIL_total", "AUDIT_TOTAL_NEW", "DAST_TOTAL_NEW"))



Even easier: check_outliers() with method = “all”
Uses multiple methods
Consensus approach: if half the methods flag it, remove it
Clean and principled

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Refit model

model_fit <- lm(CESD_total ~ PIL_total + AUDIT_TOTAL_NEW + DAST_TOTAL_NEW,
             data = clean_data) 



After removing outliers, refit
Now we have clean data
Our inferences will be more trustworthy

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Assumptions

Linearity
Independence
Normality of residuals
Equal error (“homoskedasticity”)

. . .

Additivity (more than one variable)



Back to basics
Linearity, independence, normality, homoskedasticity
Plus one new one for multiple regression: additivity
Effects of predictors shouldn’t depend on each other — unless you model interactions

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Assumptions

Additivity

Implies that for an existing model, the effect of a predictor on a response variable (whether it be linear or non-linear) is not affected by changes in other existing predictors

Add interaction if not the case





Additivity means: effect of X₁ doesn’t change across levels of X₂
If it does, you need an interaction term
We’ll cover interactions later

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Assumptions

performance::check_model(model_fit, check=c("normality", "linearity", "homogeneity", "qq", "vif"))

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Heteroskedasticity

check_heteroscedasticity(model_fit)

Warning: Heteroscedasticity (non-constant error variance) detected (p = 0.001).



We can use robust SEs
They work by changing the covariance matrix (the diagonal is the variance)
\[
\text{Var}(\epsilon) = \sigma^2 I_n = \sigma^2
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\
0 & 1 & \cdots & 0 \\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
0 & 0 & \cdots & 1
\end{bmatrix}
\]



check_heteroscedasticity() detected a problem (p = .001)
Variance isn’t constant — our standard errors are wrong
Solution: robust standard errors
They adjust the covariance matrix

title: Multiple Regression
text:
Heteroskedasticity
\[
D_{\text{HC3}} =
\begin{bmatrix}
\frac{\epsilon_1^2}{(1-h_{11})^2} & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\
0 & \frac{\epsilon_2^2}{(1-h_{22})^2} & \cdots & 0 \\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
0 & 0 & \cdots & \frac{\epsilon_n^2}{(1-h_{nn})^2}
\end{bmatrix}
\]

library(easystats) # model_paramters function
#fit model first then read into function
mp <- model_parameters(model_fit, vcov = "HC3")

title: Generalized Linear Madness: Binary Outcome Models/Logistic Regression
text:
Generalized linear model

Regression models with non-normal response likelihoods

\[\begin{align*}
  Y_i & \sim \mathrm{Dist}(\mu_i, \tau)  \\
  g(\mu_i) & = \eta_i \\
  \eta_i & = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{1i} + \beta_2 X_{2i} + \ldots
\end{align*}\]Where:

\(y\) is referenced with \(\mu\)
\(g\) is link function (in logistic regression we use logit link)

title: Generalized Linear Madness: Binary Outcome Models/Logistic Regression
section: What distribution do we use to model this process?
text:
What distribution do we use to model this process?

We assume that there is some probability p of responding correctly (or selecting what is coded as 1)
We don’t know this probability, so we want to use the data to estimate it

title: Generalized Linear Madness: Binary Outcome Models/Logistic Regression
text:
Bernoulli distribution



Distribution of a single, discrete binary outcome \[y\sim Bernoulli(p)\]


A Bernoulli distribution generates a 1 (“success”) with probability p
And a 0 (“failure”) with probability 1−p=q

\(\mu\) = E(X)=p
\(\sigma^2(X)=p(1-p)\)

title: Generalized Linear Madness: Binary Outcome Models/Logistic Regression
text:
Binomial distribution



Distribution of discrete counts of independent outcomes over a certain set of trials

\[y\sim binomial(N,p)\]

N = number of trials
p = probability of “y = 1”

\(\mu\) = E(X)=np$
\(\sigma^2(X)=np(1-p)\)
\(\sigma(X)\)=\(\sqrt{np(1-p)}\)

Generalized Linear Madness: Binary Outcome Models/Logistic Regression
text:
Logit link

Step 1

Transform probability into odds

The “odds” of an event are just the probability it happens divided by the probability it does not happen



\[\textrm{Odds} = \frac{\# \textrm{successes}}{\# \textrm{failures}}=
\frac{\# \textrm{successes}/n}{\# \textrm{failures}/n}=
\frac{p}{1-p}\]

title: Generalized Linear Madness: Binary Outcome Models/Logistic Regression
text:
Logit Link



Step 2

When we convert a probability to odds, odds always > 0

Asymmetric
Curvy

Problematic for linear model


Solution: take log of the odds

\[logit = log(\frac{p}{1-p})\]















If you look at the figure here, we have the odds scale..
P as a function of odds –> bounded to 0. P<0.5 is crammed to this region, and the rest extends to infinity

Odds are always positive and asymmetric — an odds of 2 means twice as likely but an odds of 0.5 means half as likely.
Now we can take the log


Suddenly — symmetric. Zero sits in the middle. p < 0.5 goes negative. p > 0.5 goes positive. Equal room on both sides.
This is a scale where regression works!

title: Generalized Linear Madness: Binary Outcome Models/Logistic Regression
section: Two Link Functions You Need to Know [B1]
text:
Two Link Functions You Need to Know [B1]



Logit link (today)

Maps probability \((0, 1)\) → log-odds \((-\infty, +\infty)\)

\[\text{logit}(p) = \log\frac{p}{1-p}\]

Used for: Binomial / Logistic models
Inverse (logistic function) produces the S-curve
Effect on outcome: compressed near 0 and 1




Log link (coming soon)

Maps positive values \((0, +\infty)\) → real line \((-\infty, +\infty)\)

\[\log(\mu) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X\]

Used for: Poisson / Count models
Inverse is exponentiation: \(\mu = e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1 X}\)
Effect on outcome: exponential scaling




. . .






Note



Both links solve the same problem — mapping a constrained parameter onto an unconstrained linear model. The logit handles probabilities; the log handles positive counts.

title: Generalized Linear Madness: Binary Outcome Models/Logistic Regression
text:
Best fitting squiggle

In standard linear regression we use least squares to find the best fitting line











But with binary data, we need a different approach…
Step 1: We need find where points lie on line and get corresponding logits

title: Generalized Linear Madness: Binary Outcome Models/Logistic Regression
text:
ML: Logistic Regression

Step 2: Project them onto the probability scale (rotate the log-odds line)

title: Generalized Linear Madness: Binary Outcome Models/Logistic Regression
text:
Now what?

Step 3: We keep rotating the log odds (line) and projecting data on to it and transforming into probabilities

Until we find the set of parameters that maximizes the likelihood of observing our data!

title: Generalized Linear Madness: Binary Outcome Models/Logistic Regression
text:
MLE vs. OLS

OLS minimizes sum of squared residuals
MLE finds parameter values that make observed data most probable
No closed-form solution — uses iterative algorithms (Newton-Raphson / IRLS)

text:
Reporting






Tip



We fitted a logistic model with a logit link (estimated using ML) with sex and bmipct predicting desire to lose weight (formula: lose.wt.01 ~ 1 + female+ bmipct). The model’s explanatory power is substantial (Tjur’s \(R^2\) =0.30). The probability of females wanting to lose weight was 33% higher, b= 1.86, 95% CI [1.37, 2.38], p < .001; OR = 2.98, 95% CI [3.93, 10.9]. An increase in BMI was associated with an increased probability of wanting to lose weight, b = 0.05, 95% CI [0.04, 0.06], p < .001, OR = 1.05, 95% CI [1.04, 1.06]. Looking at the average marginal effect, 1 unit increases in BMI was associated with a 80% increase in desire to lose weight.

title: Generalized Linear Madness: Binary Outcome Models/Logistic Regression
text:
Reporting Checklist

Report the link function and estimation method (e.g., logit link, ML estimation)
Report log-odds coefficients and odds ratios with 95% CIs
Report a measure of model fit (McFadden \(R^2\), Tjur \(R^2\), etc.)
Consider reporting marginal effects for practical significance
Include sample size, number of events, and events-per-variable ratio
Mention any convergence issues or model diagnostics

title: Generalized Linear Madness: Binary Outcome Models/Logistic Regression
text:
Common Mistakes

Interpreting log-odds coefficients as if they were probabilities
Forgetting that effects are non-linear on the probability scale

A 1-unit change in X does not have a constant effect on P(Y=1)

Using \(R^2\) from linear regression — use pseudo \(R^2\) measures instead
Not checking for multicollinearity (VIF still applies!)

What distribution do we use to model this process?

title: GLM & Logistic Regression (updated)
text:
Bernoulli distribution



Distribution of a single, discrete binary outcome \[y\sim Bernoulli(p)\]


A Bernoulli distribution generates a 1 (“success”) with probability p
And a 0 (“failure”) with probability 1−p=q

\(\mu\) = E(X)=p
\(\sigma^2(X)=p(1-p)\)

title: GLM & Logistic Regression (updated)
text:
Binomial distribution



Distribution of discrete counts of independent outcomes over a certain set of trials

\[y\sim binomial(N,p)\]

N = number of trials
p = probability of “y = 1”

\(\mu\) = E(X)=np$
\(\sigma^2(X)=np(1-p)\)
\(\sigma(X)\)=\(\sqrt{np(1-p)}\)

text:
Logit link

Step 1

Transform probability into odds

The “odds” of an event are just the probability it happens divided by the probability it does not happen



\[\textrm{Odds} = \frac{\# \textrm{successes}}{\# \textrm{failures}}=
\frac{\# \textrm{successes}/n}{\# \textrm{failures}/n}=
\frac{p}{1-p}\]

title: GLM & Logistic Regression (updated)
text:
Logit Link



Step 2

When we convert a probability to odds, odds always > 0

Asymmetric
Curvy

Problematic for linear model


Solution: take log of the odds

\[logit = log(\frac{p}{1-p})\]














If you look at the figure here, we have the odds scale..
P as a function of odds –> bounded to 0. P<0.5 is crammed to this region, and the rest extends to infinity

Odds are always positive and asymmetric — an odds of 2 means twice as likely but an odds of 0.5 means half as likely.
Now we can take the log


Suddenly — symmetric. Zero sits in the middle. p < 0.5 goes negative. p > 0.5 goes positive. Equal room on both sides.
This is a scale where regression works!

title: GLM & Logistic Regression (updated)
section: Two Link Functions You Need to Know [B1]
text:
Two Link Functions You Need to Know [B1]


Logit link (today)

Maps probability \((0, 1)\) → log-odds \((-\infty, +\infty)\)

\[\text{logit}(p) = \log\frac{p}{1-p}\]

Used for: Binomial / Logistic models
Inverse (logistic function) produces the S-curve
Effect on outcome: compressed near 0 and 1


Log link (coming soon)

Maps positive values \((0, +\infty)\) → real line \((-\infty, +\infty)\)

\[\log(\mu) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X\]

Used for: Poisson / Count models
Inverse is exponentiation: \(\mu = e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1 X}\)
Effect on outcome: exponential scaling









Note


Both links solve the same problem — mapping a constrained parameter onto an unconstrained linear model. The logit handles probabilities; the log handles positive counts.

text:
Now what?

Step 3: We keep rotating the log odds (line) and projecting data on to it and transforming into probabilities

Until we find the set of parameters that maximizes the likelihood of observing our data!

text:
MLE vs. OLS

OLS minimizes sum of squared residuals
MLE finds parameter values that make observed data most probable
No closed-form solution — uses iterative algorithms (Newton-Raphson / IRLS)

section: Simulation with a Data Generating Process
text:
Simulation with a Data Generating Process
8 coins. 20 tosses each.
Each coin has a small lead weight on the heads side. More lead => higher probability of heads.

set.seed(504)

# --- DATA GENERATING FUNCTION ---
# Lead weight (grams) determines each coin's bias
coins <- tibble(
  coin        = 1:8,
  lead_weight = 1:8,
  true_p      = c(0.05, 0.15, 0.30, 0.45, 0.55, 0.70, 0.85, 0.95)
)

# Flip each coin 20 times (individual tosses)
individual <- coins %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(outcomes = list(rbinom(20, 1, true_p))) %>%
  unnest(outcomes) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  group_by(coin) %>%
  mutate(toss = row_number()) %>%
  ungroup()

# Aggregate to counts (same data, summarized)
tosses <- individual %>%
  group_by(coin, lead_weight, true_p) %>%
  summarize(
    heads      = sum(outcomes),
    tails      = 20 - heads,
    observed_p = heads / 20,
    .groups    = "drop"
  )

Can we transform the data?
We need a scale where the relationship is linear. Can we just… transform?

Individual 0/1?

Aggregated proportions?

Works fine.



So we have two options.

title: GLM & Logistic Regression (updated)
text:
Option 1 works — but has limits


Log-odds scale is linear ✓ — OLS would work here.


But this needs groups to compute proportions from. Our coins had that — 20 tosses at each weight. What if we wanted predictors like spin rate, etc. that can vary across tosses ?


Option 1 requires aggregation which requires clear grouping / binning (which can be lossy).

title: GLM & Logistic Regression (updated)
section: Option 2: Let the model handle it
text:
Option 2: Let the model handle it
glm() doesn’t transform your data. It works from the other direction.


Propose a line in log-odds: \(\;\text{logit}(\hat{p}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x\)




Convert to predicted probabilities: \(\;\hat{p} = \text{plogis}(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x)\)




Score against your raw data (0/1s or counts) — “how likely is what I observed?”



The model builds its line in log-odds space. Then it comes to your data to check its work.

title: GLM & Logistic Regression (updated)
section: Option 2: The model’s predictions gets a new scale
text:
Option 2: The model’s predictions gets a new scale
The model’s predicted probability \(\hat{p}\) can be expressed \(\hat{p}\) on three scales:


Probability

Bounded: \([0, 1]\)
S-shaped
What you want to estimate and interpret
Can’t use OLS


Odds

Bounded: \([0, +\infty)\)
\(\frac{\hat{p}}{1-\hat{p}}\)
Still undesirable for OLS


Log-odds

Unbounded: \((-\infty, +\infty)\)
\(\log\frac{\hat{p}}{1-\hat{p}}\)
Model is happy because now there’s a Linear relationship
And you’re happy because you can map it to an interpetable parameter

title: GLM & Logistic Regression (updated)
text:
What is Maximum Likelihood?
In OLS — we minimize the squared residuals. Closed-form solution.
With binary data — squared residuals don’t make sense. Instead:

Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE)
Find the parameter values that make the observed data least surprising/ most likely.


The logic:

Propose some parameter values (\(\beta_0\), \(\beta_1\))
Ask: if these were the true values, how probable is the data I actually got?
Score that probability — the likelihood
Repeat with different values until the likelihood is as high as possible



The parameters at the peak = the maximum likelihood estimates.

title: GLM & Logistic Regression (updated)
text:
MLE for logistic regression
How does MLE apply to our problem?

The model proposes a straight line in log-odds: \(\;\text{logit}(p) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot \text{lead_weight}\)


Converts to probabilities: \(\;\hat{p}_i = \text{plogis}(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i)\) for each observation


Scores against the data:

Observation got a 1 ●? Score = \(\hat{p}_i\) — higher is better
Observation got a 0 ●? Score = \(1 - \hat{p}_i\) — higher is better



Total likelihood = multiply all the scores: \(\;\;L = \prod_{i=1}^{n} \hat{p}_i^{y_i}(1-\hat{p}_i)^{1-y_i}\)


Try thousands of lines → find the one with the highest \(L\).
That line’s \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\) are your estimates.

title: GLM & Logistic Regression (updated)
section: Where does the score come from?
text:
Where does the score come from?
Model predicts \(\hat{p} = 0.88\) for the 6g coin. It lands heads. How likely was that?

*Bernoulli Likelihood formula:**
\[L(\hat{p}_i) = \hat{p}_i^{\,y_i} \cdot (1 - \hat{p}_i)^{1-y_i}\]
\(y = 1\): just \(\hat{p}\). \(\;\;\) \(y = 0\): just \(1 - \hat{p}\).


Two observations? Multiply. 160 observations? Multiply all scores → likelihood.
But 160 tiny numbers multiplied → computer underflow. So we take the log:
\[\log {L} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left[ y_i \log(\hat{p}_i) + (1 - y_i) \log(1 - \hat{p}_i) \right]\]
Same ranking and same peak (what we need for max). And numerically stable.

Build the likelihood from a single observation. Left panel: if the coin lands heads (Y=1), the likelihood IS the predicted probability. The grey line is L(p̂) = p̂ — a straight line. At p̂ = 0.88, the green dot reads off 0.88. High prediction for an event that happened → high score. Right panel: same prediction, but tails (Y=0). Now L(p̂) = 1 − p̂. At p̂ = 0.88, the red dot reads off 0.12. The model predicted 88% heads but got tails — low score, the model was surprised.
The formula combines both. When y=1, the exponents collapse to p̂. When y=0, they collapse to 1−p̂.
For multiple observations, multiply. But 160 numbers between 0 and 1 multiplied together → astronomically small. Like 10⁻⁴⁷. Computers can’t handle that — underflow. So we take the log. Log turns products into sums. Same ranking — if likelihood A beats likelihood B, log-likelihood A also beats log-likelihood B. Same peak. Just stable arithmetic. (J: Let me show you exactly where the score comes from. Left panel — the coin lands heads. The likelihood function for a single heads is just a straight line: the higher your predicted probability, the higher your score. Our model predicted 0.88, so the score is 0.88. Green dot, right there. Right panel — same prediction, but tails happened. Now the likelihood goes the other way — high prediction for something that didn’t happen means a LOW score. 0.12. The model was wrong and the score shows it. The formula at the bottom just wraps both cases into one expression. Now — multiply 160 of these scores together and you get the likelihood. Problem is, 160 numbers less than 1 multiplied together gives you something tiny — like 10 to the negative 47. Computers can’t handle that. So we take the log. Addition instead of multiplication. Same answer, same winner, just numbers your computer can actually store.)

title: GLM & Logistic Regression (updated)
text:
Scoring each guess
For each observation:

If \(Y_i = 1\) (heads ●): score = \(\hat{p}_i\) — higher is better
If \(Y_i = 0\) (tails ●): score = \(1 - \hat{p}_i\) — higher is better

Log-likelihood = sum of log(scores) across all observations

compute_ll <- function(b0, b1, data) {
  p_hat <- plogis(b0 + b1 * data$lead_weight)
  sum(data$outcomes * log(p_hat) + (1 - data$outcomes) * log(1 - p_hat))
}

tibble(
  Guess = c("A: shallow (red)", "B: moderate (blue)", "C: steep (purple)"),
  `β₀` = c(-0.5, -2.0, -4.0),
  `β₁` = c(0.1, 0.5, 1.2),
  `Log-likelihood` = round(c(
    compute_ll(-0.5, 0.1, individual),
    compute_ll(-2.0, 0.5, individual),
    compute_ll(-4.0, 1.2, individual)
  ), 2)
) %>% knitr::kable()

Coefficient effect size: Odd’s Ratio

We can take the exp() of the log odds and get OR

The odds of Y for group X (females) are expected to be exp(\(b_1\)) times the odds of Y for the baseline group

Greater than 1: One unit increase, the event is more likely to occur
Less than 1: One unit increase, the event is less likely to occur
Equals 1: One unit increase, the likelihood of the event does not change

We can describe the OR in terms of percentage increase/decrease

title: GLM & Logistic Regression (updated)
text:
Reporting






Tip


We fitted a logistic model with a logit link (estimated using ML) with sex and bmipct predicting desire to lose weight (formula: lose.wt.01 ~ 1 + female+ bmipct). The model’s explanatory power is substantial (Tjur’s \(R^2\) =0.30). The probability of females wanting to lose weight was 33% higher, b= 1.86, 95% CI [1.37, 2.38], p < .001; OR = 2.98, 95% CI [3.93, 10.9]. An increase in BMI was associated with an increased probability of wanting to lose weight, b = 0.05, 95% CI [0.04, 0.06], p < .001, OR = 1.05, 95% CI [1.04, 1.06]. Looking at the average marginal effect, 1 unit increases in BMI was associated with a 80% increase in desire to lose weight.

title: GLM & Logistic Regression (updated)
text:
Reporting Checklist

Report the link function and estimation method (e.g., logit link, ML estimation)
Report log-odds coefficients and odds ratios with 95% CIs
Report a measure of model fit (McFadden \(R^2\), Tjur \(R^2\), etc.)
Consider reporting marginal effects for practical significance
Include sample size, number of events, and events-per-variable ratio
Mention any convergence issues or model diagnostics

title: GLM & Logistic Regression (updated)
text:
Common Mistakes

Interpreting log-odds coefficients as if they were probabilities
Forgetting that effects are non-linear on the probability scale

A 1-unit change in X does not have a constant effect on P(Y=1)

Using \(R^2\) from linear regression — use pseudo \(R^2\) measures instead
Not checking for multicollinearity (VIF still applies!)

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
section: What is a data generating process?
text:
What is a data generating process?
The process that produced your data.

Last semester — every simulation you wrote was one.
Pick a distribution. Pick parameters. Generate data.


Last week — logistic regression was one.
Lead weight → probability → coin flips.

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
section: A model (class) is a family of DGPs
text:
A model (class) is a family of DGPs
A model = a structure with free parameters.

Each choice of parameters → a different member.


\[Y_i \sim \text{Normal}(\mu_i, \sigma), \quad \mu_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i\]



\(\beta_0 = 50, \beta_1 = 0.3, \sigma = 10\) → one member
\(\beta_0 = 40, \beta_1 = 0.8, \sigma = 5\) → another member



Same family. Different members.

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
Two families you already know


Linear model
\[
\begin{align}
Y_i &\sim \text{Normal}(\mu_i, \sigma) \\
\mu_i &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i
\end{align}
\]

Logistic model
\[
\begin{align}
Y_i &\sim \text{Bernoulli}(p_i) \\
\text{logit}(p_i) &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i
\end{align}
\]


Same structure:

you specify parameters
at each X, the parameters produce a different distribution
data gets drawn from it (the ~ ; captures randomness)

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
The DGP runs forward (parameters → data)
We fix the parameters. And generate data.

“If \(\beta_0 = 50\), \(\beta_1 = 0.3\), \(\sigma = 10\) — what grades would I see?”
rnorm(n = 33, mean = 50 + 0.3 * avgView, sd = 10)



Parameters are known (you chose them)
Data varies (different every time you simulate)
This is simulation — r functions: rnorm(), rbinom()

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
What ~ means
\(Y_i \sim \text{Binomial}(n, \theta)\) means:
\[p(Y = k \mid \theta) = \binom{n}{k}\theta^k(1-\theta)^{n-k}\]

“If \(\theta = 0.6\) — what data can come out, and how often?”


In R,
dbinom(0:5, size = 5, prob = 0.6)


These sum to 1. Every outcome covered. A proper distribution.


This is \(p(\text{data} \mid \theta)\).

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
Inference runs backward (data → parameters)
You observed 3 heads out of 5.
Which member of the family produced them?

Data are fixed. Parameters are unknown.


Two strategies:



MLE — find the best-scoring member




Bayes — get a distribution over all plausible members

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
section: How do we score the members?
text:
How do we score the members?
Fix the data. Ask each member: how well do you explain this?

You got 3 heads out of 5.


\(\theta = 0.6\) → score: 0.346
\(\theta = 0.5\) → score: 0.312
\(\theta = 0.2\) → score: 0.051


Higher score = that member explains the data better.

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
section: How do we score the members?
text:
How do we score the members?
Fix the data. Ask each member: how well do you explain this?

You got 3 heads out of 5.


\(\theta = 0.6\) → score: 0.346
\(\theta = 0.5\) → score: 0.312
\(\theta = 0.2\) → score: 0.051


Higher score = that member explains the data better.

Data fixed at 3 heads. Read down the column.


Peak at \(\theta = 0.6\). That’s what MLE does — pick the peak.


Sum = 1.144. Not 1. This column is not a distribution.
True bias: \(\theta = 0.5\). You flip 5 times. You get 4 heads.


Read down the “4 heads” column:

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
“But it’s the same table/number!”
dbinom(3, 5, 0.6) = 0.346 in both tables. So why does it matter?

Try to make a statement:


Forward: “There’s a 35% chance of getting 3 heads.” ✓


Backward: “There’s a **___% chance** that \(\theta\) is 0.6.”


You can’t fill in the blank.
The scores don’t add to 1. 0.346 is not a percentage here.


That blank is \(p(\theta \mid \text{data})\). We don’t have it yet.

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
Probability vs. likelihood
Same formula: \(p(\text{data} \mid \theta)\). Different direction.



Read across a row

\(\theta\) fixed, data varies
Sums to 1 ✓
Probability


Read down a column

Data fixed, \(\theta\) varies
Does not sum to 1 ✗
Likelihood \(L(\theta)\)




Rows = distribution. Columns = scoring function.

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
The likelihood is not enough
We want \(p(\theta \mid \text{data})\) — a distribution.

The likelihood finds the peak. That’s MLE.


But it can’t fill in the blank: “___% chance \(\theta\) is between 0.4 and 0.8.”


We need one more ingredient.

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
section: You know things before seeing data
text:
You know things before seeing data

You’re flipping a coin — not rolling a die, not drawing cards.


Most coins are roughly fair. \(\theta\) is probably near 0.5.


\(\theta = 0.0\) or \(\theta = 1.0\)? A two-headed or two-tailed coin? Possible — but unlikely.


The likelihood doesn’t have this knowledge. It just scores.

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
A prior distribution
Which \(\theta\) values are plausible — before you flip?
\[p(\theta)\]

“Most coins are fair-ish” → prior peaked near 0.5


“I have no idea” → flat prior, all \(\theta\) equally plausible


“This coin came from a magic shop” → prior allows extreme values


Unlike the likelihood — the prior is a distribution. Sums to 1.

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
Bayes’ rule
\[p(\theta \mid \text{data}) \;\propto\; \underbrace{p(\theta)}_{\text{Prior}} \;\times\; \underbrace{L(\theta)}_{\text{Likelihood}}\]

Prior (distribution) × Likelihood (scoring function) = Posterior (distribution)



Prior — what you believed before
Likelihood — what the data say
Posterior — your updated belief



The posterior is \(p(\theta \mid \text{data})\).
Now you can fill in the blank.

The coin posterior

Posterior sums to 1. Now it’s a distribution.


“There’s a 30% chance \(\theta\) is 0.6.” The blank is filled.

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
Bayes’ rule
\[p(\theta \mid \text{data}) \;\propto\; \underbrace{p(\theta)}_{\text{Prior}} \;\times\; \underbrace{L(\theta)}_{\text{Likelihood}}\]

Prior (distribution) × Likelihood (scoring function) = Posterior (distribution)



Prior — what you believed before
Likelihood — what the data say
Posterior — your updated belief



The full version:
\[p(\theta \mid \text{data}) = \frac{p(\theta) \times L(\theta)}{\sum_{\theta} p(\theta) \times L(\theta)}\]
The denominator just makes it sum to 1.

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
Three ingredients


Prior \(p(\theta)\)
Belief before data
Distribution ✓

Likelihood \(L(\theta)\)
What data say
Not a distribution ✗

Posterior \(p(\theta \mid \text{data})\)
Updated belief
Distribution ✓



Both high → posterior high
Either low → posterior pulled down
With lots of data — likelihood dominates
With little data — prior matters more

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
section: Why can’t we just compute it?
text:
Why can’t we just compute it?
In principle — just multiply prior × likelihood at every \(\theta\).

For the coin with 5 values of \(\theta\)? Easy. Do it by hand.


But real models have continuous parameters — every \(\theta\) between 0 and 1.
\[p(\theta \mid \text{data}) = \frac{p(\theta) \times L(\theta)}{\int p(\theta) \times L(\theta) \, d\theta}\]


That denominator — integrate over every possible \(\theta\).


1 parameter → fine. 3 → hard. 20 → forget it.


Solution: don’t compute it. Sample from it.
That’s MCMC. That’s brms.

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
What does “sample from it” mean?
We can’t write down \(p(\theta \mid \text{data})\) as a formula.

But we can generate thousands of \(\theta\) values that behave as if they came from it.


Imagine drawing 10,000 values of \(\theta\) from the posterior:

~300 of them would be near 0.6
~270 near 0.5
~45 near 0.2
Almost none near 0.0



The histogram of those draws is the posterior.
No formula needed. Just draws.


That’s what MCMC does. That’s what brms gives you.

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
section: What Bayes gives you that MLE doesn’t
text:
What Bayes gives you that MLE doesn’t









MLE
Bayes




Point estimate
✓ (peak)
✓ (posterior mean/median)


Uncertainty
SE from curvature
Full distribution


Probability statements
✗
“95% chance β₁ ∈ [0.1, 0.5]”


Prior knowledge
✗
✓


Small samples
Unstable (due to sampling error)
Priors stabilize estimates


Evidence FOR null
✗
✓ (Bayes Factors)

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text: The rise of Bayesian statistics

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
Why now?


Technology

Faster computers
Better algorithms (MCMC -> HMC)
Accessible software (brms, Stan)


Frustration

Can’t incorporate prior knowledge
p-values don’t answer what we want
Can’t find evidence FOR the null
Replication crisis

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
Bayesian statistics as a tool



Google “Bayesian” → philosophical wars
Subjective vs. objective. Frequentist vs. Bayesian.
Interesting. Not our focus.

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
Two views of probability


Frequentist
Probability = long-run frequency.
“If I repeated this experiment forever, 60% of the time I’d get heads.”
. . .
Parameters are fixed but unknown.
Data are random.
Only data get probability statements.

Bayesian
Probability = degree of belief.
“I’m 60% sure this coin is biased toward heads.”
. . .
Parameters are uncertain — they get distributions.
Data are fixed (you observed them).
Parameters get probability statements.

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
Belief updating: an example
Let’s watch Bayes’ rule work — step by step.

What proportion of people are dog people?



Data: 0 = cat person, 1 = dog person
Parameter: \(\theta\) = proportion of dog people
Sample: 5 people



Same structure as the coin — just a different question.

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
Step 1: State your prior


People vary in how strongly they state prior beliefs.



Informative → “I’m pretty sure it’s near 0.5”
Weakly informative → “Probably between 0.2 and 0.8”
Non-informative → “I have no idea”



Most researchers use weakly informative priors.

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
Step 2: Your prior makes predictions
Before seeing data — what does each model predict?


Narrow prior → specific predictions.
Wide prior → anything is plausible.

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
Step 3: Collect data


3 out of 5 are dog people.
Everything before this happened without data.
Now we update.

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
Step 4: Which model predicted better?
The marginal likelihood — how plausible is the observed data under each model?


Go back to each model’s predictions. Evaluate at the observed data.
The ratio of these = the Bayes Factor.

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
Bayes Factors
How much did the data change your mind?
\[BF_{12} = \frac{P(\text{data} \mid M_1)}{P(\text{data} \mid M_2)}\]


\(BF > 1\) → data favor \(M_1\)
\(BF < 1\) → data favor \(M_2\)
\(BF = 1\) → data equally consistent with both



Unlike p-values — BFs can provide evidence for the null.

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
Step 5: Update → Posterior


The wide prior (blue) gets reshaped — narrower, pulled toward the data.


The spike prior (green) doesn’t budge.
If you rule something out completely, no data can bring it back.

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
Prior → Posterior


The posterior sits between prior and likelihood.
With more data — pulled toward the likelihood.
With less data — stays closer to the prior.

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
Credible intervals
The posterior gives you what you always wanted from confidence intervals:

“With 95% probability, \(\theta\) lies within this interval.”













This is a direct probability statement about the parameter.
Not “if we repeated the experiment…”

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
Same recipe, more parameters









Coin
Regression




Model
\(Y \sim \text{Binomial}(n, \theta)\)
\(Y \sim \text{Normal}(\mu_i, \sigma)\)


Parameters
\(\theta\)
\(\beta_0, \beta_1, \sigma\)


Prior
\(p(\theta)\)
\(p(\beta_0), p(\beta_1), p(\sigma)\)


Likelihood
Score each \(\theta\)
Score each \((\beta_0, \beta_1, \sigma)\)


Posterior
\(p(\theta \mid \text{data})\)
\(p(\beta_0, \beta_1, \sigma \mid \text{data})\)




More parameters. Same recipe.


brms handles all of it.

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
Computing a likelihood
compute_ll <- function(b0, b1, data) {
  p_hat <- plogis(b0 + b1 * data$lead_weight)
  sum(data$outcomes * log(p_hat) + 
      (1 - data$outcomes) * log(1 - p_hat))
}

Same idea — many parameters, score each combination.


The linear model has one too — swap in dnorm().

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
section: The likelihood for a linear model
text:
The likelihood for a linear model
\[Y_i \sim \text{Normal}(\mu_i, \sigma), \quad \mu_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i\]
Say \(\beta_0 = 50\), \(\beta_1 = 0.3\), \(\sigma = 10\):


Student watches 30 min → predicted mean = \(50 + 0.3(30) = 59\)
Actual grade = 65
Score: dnorm(65, mean = 59, sd = 10) ≈ 0.03



Do this for every student. Multiply. That’s the likelihood.
Different parameters → different score.

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
Priors for regression
Same logic as the coin — just different parameters.


Grades are 0–100. \(\beta_0\) can’t be 500. → \(\beta_0 \sim \text{Normal}(50, 20)\)




Watching lectures shouldn’t hurt. \(\beta_1\) probably isn’t −20. → \(\beta_1 \sim \text{Normal}(0, 5)\)




\(\sigma\) must be positive, probably not 1000. → \(\sigma \sim \text{Half-Cauchy}(0, 10)\)



MLE ignores all of this. Bayes encodes it.

Declaring Priors
You have to identify:

Distribution of every statistic you want to estimate, including the dependent variable and each parameter of its distribution

(e.g., DV ~ N( \(\mu\) , \(\sigma\)))

Expected values for the location and spread of the distributions

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
How to choose

People argue about priors

Where do they come from?
Priors differ in how informative they are
Priors differ in how ‘proper’ they are

Creates camps:

“Subjective Bayesians” vs. “Objective Bayesians” vs. “Empirical Bayesians” vs. “Pragmatic Bayesians”

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
Informativeness of priors

Informative Priors (“Subjective Bayesians”)

Prior distributions that are specific about the values of model parameters (e.g., true correlation ≈ N(μ = -0.5)

Non-informative Priors (“Objective Bayesians”)

Priors that let data speak for themselves; invariant to transformation

Weakly-informative priors (“WIP”; Most Bayesians)

Specifying the distribution (e.g., Normal), with starting values known to bias estimates the least

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
Informativeness of priors

People vary in how strongly they state their prior beliefs
If you state your belief strongly

E.g., the true correlation is ~N(0.3, 0.06)

Pitfall: Your beliefs have greater influence over the shape of the posterior distribution


If you state your belief weakly

E.g., true correlation is equally likely at any real value between -1 and 1

Pitfall: You run the risk of overestimating the relative densities of the posterior distribution to the prior distribution

Bayes factors



Frequentists have p values
Bayesians have Bayes factors (BF)

Tells you how much more likely the observed data are under one model than under another model
Can be interpreted as degree of relative evidence for a model
\[\text{Bayes factor} (BF) = \frac{P(\mathcal{D}|M_1)}{P(\mathcal{D}|M_2)}\]









\(BF_{12}\) > 1: More evidence for M1
\(BF_{12}\) < 1: More evidence for M2

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
Bayesian models as psychological theory
The claim: people behave as if they do Bayesian inference.


Language: Children infer word meanings from few examples (Xu & Tenenbaum, 2007)




Perception: The brain combines noisy sensory input with prior expectations (Knill & Pouget, 2004)




Causal reasoning: People learn causal structure from sparse evidence (Griffiths & Tenenbaum, 2005)




Motor control: You catch a ball by combining visual uncertainty with learned priors (Körding & Wolpert, 2004)



These are theories about cognition — testable, debatable, sometimes wrong.
Our course: Bayes as a screwdriver, not a theory of the hand.

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
Computing the posterior

Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampler!
Given possible priors and your data, a computer uses a Monte Carlo sampling technique to build stochastic Markov Chains, a process referred to as MCMC
We run multiple chains (e.g., 4 chains in brms) with equal numbers of iterations (e.g., 5000 iterations) in each chain to estimate convergence/stability
MCMC chains contain samples from the posterior distribution of the theory given the data

Sample size does not affect estimates as much as it does the likelihood

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
section: What is a data generating process?
text:
What is a data generating process?
The process that produced your data.

Last semester — every simulation you wrote was one.
Pick a distribution. Pick parameters. Generate data.


Last week — logistic regression was one.
Lead weight → probability → coin flips.

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
section: A model (class) is a family of DGPs
text:
A model (class) is a family of DGPs
A model = a structure with free parameters.

Each choice of parameters → a different member of the family.


\[Y_i \sim \text{Normal}(\mu_i, \sigma), \quad \mu_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i\]



\(\beta_0 = 50, \beta_1 = 0.3, \sigma = 10\) → one member
\(\beta_0 = 40, \beta_1 = 0.8, \sigma = 5\) → another member

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
Two families you already know


Linear model
\[
\begin{align}
Y_i &\sim \text{Normal}(\mu_i, \sigma) \\
\mu_i &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i
\end{align}
\]

Logistic model
\[
\begin{align}
Y_i &\sim \text{Bernoulli}(p_i) \\
\text{logit}(p_i) &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i
\end{align}
\]


Model structure:

you specify parameters
at each X, the parameters produce a different distribution
data gets drawn from it (the ~ ; captures randomness)

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
The DGP runs forward (parameters → data)
We fix the parameters. And generate data.

“If \(\beta_0 = 50\), \(\beta_1 = 0.3\), \(\sigma = 10\) — what grades would I see?”
rnorm(n = 33, mean = 50 + 0.3 * avgView, sd = 10)



Parameters are known/ fixed by you
Data varies (different in each simulation)
r functions: rnorm(), rbinom()

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
What ~ means
\(Y_i \sim \text{Binomial}(n, \theta)\) means you are sampling n points from:
\[p(Y = k \mid \theta) = \binom{n}{k}\theta^k(1-\theta)^{n-k}\]

Now you can ask questions like “If \(\theta = 0.6\) — what data/outcomes are possible, and how likely are they?”


dbinom(0:5, size = 5, prob = 0.6)
These sum to 1. . . .
The probability of each outcome is covered.
You get a proper probability distribution.


This is \(p(\text{data} \mid \theta)\).

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
Inference runs backward (data → parameters)
You observed 3 heads out of 5 tosses.
Which model parameterization produced these observations?

Here, data are fixed.
But, parameters are unknown.


Two strategies for guessing:



MLE — find the best-scoring row in the table




Bayes — get a distribution over all plausible members

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
section: How do we score the members?
text:
How do we score the members?
Fix the data.
In each row, ask: how often does one expect the outcome?

We observe 3 heads out of 5.


\(\theta = 0.6\) → score: 0.346
\(\theta = 0.5\) → score: 0.312
\(\theta = 0.2\) → score: 0.051


Higher score => that row explains the data better.

\(\theta = 0.5\) → score: 0.312
\(\theta = 0.2\) → score: 0.051


Higher score = that member explains the data better.

4 heads

With 5 flips — the peak is noisy. The best-scoring member isn’t necessarily the true one.

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
“But it’s the same table/number!”
dbinom(3, 5, 0.6) = 0.346 in both tables. So why does it matter?

Try to make a statement:


Forward: “There’s a 35% chance of getting 3 heads.” ✓


Backward: “There’s a **___% chance** that \(\theta\) is 0.6.”


You can’t fill in the blank.
The scores don’t add to 1. 0.346 is not a percentage here.


That blank is \(p(\theta \mid \text{data})\). We don’t have it yet.

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
Probability vs. likelihood
Same formula: \(p(\text{data} \mid \theta)\). Different direction.



Read across a row

\(\theta\) fixed, data varies
Sums to 1 ✓
Probability


Read down a column

Data fixed, \(\theta\) varies
Does not sum to 1 ✗
Likelihood \(L(\theta)\)




Rows = distribution. Columns = scoring function.

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
The likelihood is not enough
We want \(p(\theta \mid \text{data})\) — a distribution.

The likelihood finds the peak. That’s MLE.


But it can’t fill in the blank: “___% chance \(\theta\) is between 0.4 and 0.8.”

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
section: You know things before seeing data
text:
You know things before seeing data

You’re flipping a coin — not rolling a die, not drawing cards.


Most coins are roughly fair. \(\theta\) is probably near 0.5.


\(\theta = 0.0\) or \(\theta = 1.0\)? Possible — but highly unlikely.


The likelihood doesn’t have this knowledge.
It just scores based on \(P(D|\theta_i)\)

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
A prior distribution
Which \(\theta\) values are plausible — before you flip?
\[p(\theta)\]

“Most coins are fair-ish” → prior peaked near 0.5


“I have no idea” → flat prior, all \(\theta\) equally plausible


“This coin came from a magic shop” → prior allows extreme values


Unlike the likelihood — the prior is a distribution. Sums to 1.

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
Bayes’ rule
\[p(\theta \mid \text{data}) \;\propto\; \underbrace{p(\theta)}_{\text{Prior}} \;\times\; \underbrace{L(\theta)}_{\text{Likelihood}}\]

Prior (distribution) × Likelihood (scoring function) = Posterior (distribution)



Prior — what you believed before
Likelihood — what the data say
Posterior — your updated belief



The posterior is \(p(\theta \mid \text{data})\).
Now you can fill in the blank.

Posterior sums to 1. Now it’s a distribution.


“There’s a 30% chance \(\theta\) is 0.6.” The blank is filled.

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
Bayes’ rule
\[p(\theta \mid \text{data}) \;\propto\; \underbrace{p(\theta)}_{\text{Prior}} \;\times\; \underbrace{L(\theta)}_{\text{Likelihood}}\]

Prior (distribution) × Likelihood (scoring function) = Posterior (distribution)



Prior — what you believed before
Likelihood — what the data say
Posterior — your updated belief



The full version:
\[p(\theta \mid \text{data}) = \frac{p(\theta) \times L(\theta)}{\sum_{\theta} p(\theta) \times L(\theta)}\]
The denominator just makes it sum to 1.

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
Three ingredients


Prior \(p(\theta)\)
Belief before data
Distribution ✓

Likelihood \(L(\theta)\)
What data say
Not a distribution ✗

Posterior \(p(\theta \mid \text{data})\)
Updated belief
Distribution ✓



Both high → posterior high
Either low → posterior pulled down
With lots of data — likelihood dominates
With little data — prior matters more

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
section: Why can’t we just compute it?
text:
Why can’t we just compute it?
In principle — just multiply prior × likelihood at every \(\theta\).

But most models in practice have continuous parameters — every \(\theta\) between 0 and 1.
\[p(\theta \mid \text{data}) = \frac{p(\theta) \times L(\theta)}{\int p(\theta) \times L(\theta) \, d\theta}\]


The denominator integrates over every possible \(\theta\).


1 parameter → easy.
3 → hard.
20 → forget it.


Solution: don’t compute it. Sample from it. . . . Probabilistic programming languages let you do this more easily.

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
What does “sample from it” mean?
We can’t write down \(p(\theta \mid \text{data})\) as a formula.

But we can generate thousands of \(\theta\) values that behave as if they came from it.


Imagine drawing 10,000 values of \(\theta\) from the posterior:

~300 of them would be near 0.6
~270 near 0.5
~45 near 0.2
Almost none near 0.0



The histogram of those draws is the posterior.
We can compute probabilities now without the formula/ without knowing the likelihood function!

Technology

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
Bayesian statistics as a tool



Google “Bayesian” → philosophical wars
Subjective vs. objective. Frequentist vs. Bayesian.
Interesting. Not our focus.

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
Two views of probability


Frequentist
Probability = long-run frequency.
“If I repeated this experiment forever, 60% of the time I’d get heads.”
. . .
Parameters are fixed but unknown.
Data are random.
Only data get probability statements.

Bayesian
Probability = degree of belief.
“I’m 60% sure this coin is biased toward heads.”
. . .
Parameters are uncertain — they get distributions.
Data are fixed (you observed them).
Parameters get probability statements.

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
Belief updating: an example
Let’s watch Bayes’ rule work — step by step.

What proportion of people are dog people?



Data: 0 = cat person, 1 = dog person
Parameter: \(\theta\) = proportion of dog people
Sample: 5 people



Same structure as the coin — just a different question.

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
Step 1: State your prior


People vary in how strongly they state prior beliefs.



Informative → “I’m pretty sure it’s near 0.5”
Weakly informative → “Probably between 0.2 and 0.8”
Non-informative → “I have no idea”



Most researchers use weakly informative priors.

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
Step 2: Your prior makes predictions
Before seeing data — what does each model predict?


Narrow prior → specific predictions.
Wide prior → anything is plausible.

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
Step 3: Collect data


3 out of 5 are dog people.
Everything before this happened without data.
Now we update.

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
Step 4: Which model predicted better?
The marginal likelihood — how plausible is the observed data under each model?


Go back to each model’s predictions. Evaluate at the observed data.
The ratio of these = the Bayes Factor.

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
Bayes Factors
How much did the data change your mind?
\[BF_{12} = \frac{P(\text{data} \mid M_1)}{P(\text{data} \mid M_2)}\]


\(BF > 1\) → data favor \(M_1\)
\(BF < 1\) → data favor \(M_2\)
\(BF = 1\) → data equally consistent with both



Unlike p-values — BFs can provide evidence for the null.

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
Step 5: Update → Posterior


The wide prior (blue) gets reshaped — narrower, pulled toward the data.


The spike prior (green) doesn’t budge.
If you rule something out completely, no data can bring it back.

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
Prior → Posterior


The posterior sits between prior and likelihood.
With more data — pulled toward the likelihood.
With less data — stays closer to the prior.

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
Credible intervals
The posterior gives you what you always wanted from confidence intervals:

“With 95% probability, \(\theta\) lies within this interval.”













This is a direct probability statement about the parameter.
Not “if we repeated the experiment…”

\(Y \sim \text{Binomial}(n, \theta)\)
\(Y \sim \text{Normal}(\mu_i, \sigma)\)


Parameters
\(\theta\)
\(\beta_0, \beta_1, \sigma\)


Prior
\(p(\theta)\)
\(p(\beta_0), p(\beta_1), p(\sigma)\)


Likelihood
Score each \(\theta\)
Score each \((\beta_0, \beta_1, \sigma)\)

\(p(\theta \mid \text{data})\)

More parameters. Same recipe.


brms handles all of it.

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
Computing a likelihood
compute_ll <- function(b0, b1, data) {
  p_hat <- plogis(b0 + b1 * data$lead_weight)
  sum(data$outcomes * log(p_hat) + 
      (1 - data$outcomes) * log(1 - p_hat))
}

Same idea — many parameters, score each combination.


The linear model has one too — swap in dnorm().

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
section: The likelihood for a linear model
text:
The likelihood for a linear model
\[Y_i \sim \text{Normal}(\mu_i, \sigma), \quad \mu_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i\]
Say \(\beta_0 = 50\), \(\beta_1 = 0.3\), \(\sigma = 10\):


Student watches 30 min → predicted mean = \(50 + 0.3(30) = 59\)
Actual grade = 65
Score: dnorm(65, mean = 59, sd = 10) ≈ 0.03



Do this for every student. Multiply. That’s the likelihood.
Different parameters → different score.

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
Priors for regression
Same logic as the coin — just different parameters.


Grades are 0–100. \(\beta_0\) can’t be 500. → \(\beta_0 \sim \text{Normal}(50, 20)\)




Watching lectures shouldn’t hurt. \(\beta_1\) probably isn’t −20. → \(\beta_1 \sim \text{Normal}(0, 5)\)




\(\sigma\) must be positive, probably not 1000. → \(\sigma \sim \text{Half-Cauchy}(0, 10)\)



MLE ignores all of this. Bayes encodes it.

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
Declaring Priors
You have to identify:

Distribution of every statistic you want to estimate, including the dependent variable and each parameter of its distribution

(e.g., DV ~ N( \(\mu\) , \(\sigma\)))

Expected values for the location and spread of the distributions

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
How to choose

People argue about priors

Where do they come from?
Priors differ in how informative they are
Priors differ in how ‘proper’ they are

Creates camps:

“Subjective Bayesians” vs. “Objective Bayesians” vs. “Empirical Bayesians” vs. “Pragmatic Bayesians”

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
Informativeness of priors

Informative Priors (“Subjective Bayesians”)

Prior distributions that are specific about the values of model parameters (e.g., true correlation ≈ N(μ = -0.5)

Non-informative Priors (“Objective Bayesians”)

Priors that let data speak for themselves; invariant to transformation

Weakly-informative priors (“WIP”; Most Bayesians)

Specifying the distribution (e.g., Normal), with starting values known to bias estimates the least

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
Informativeness of priors

People vary in how strongly they state their prior beliefs
If you state your belief strongly

E.g., the true correlation is ~N(0.3, 0.06)

Pitfall: Your beliefs have greater influence over the shape of the posterior distribution


If you state your belief weakly

E.g., true correlation is equally likely at any real value between -1 and 1

Pitfall: You run the risk of overestimating the relative densities of the posterior distribution to the prior distribution

text:
Bayesian belief updating

Prior odds

Compares the relative plausibility of two models before data collection


\[\frac{p(M1)}{p(M2)}\]

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
Bayesian belief updating

Prior prediction distribution

Makes a prediction about plausibility of the data

What is the probability to observe 0, 1, 2, … dog people in a random sample of 5 people given our model?

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
Bayesian belief updating

Marginal Likelihood

How plausible are the observed data under the model?

Evaluation of the prior predictive distribution at the observed data

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
Bayes factors



Frequentists have p values
Bayesians have Bayes factors (BF)

Tells you how much more likely the observed data are under one model than under another model
Can be interpreted as degree of relative evidence for a model
\[\text{Bayes factor} (BF) = \frac{P(\mathcal{D}|M_1)}{P(\mathcal{D}|M_2)}\]









\(BF_{12}\) > 1: More evidence for M1
\(BF_{12}\) < 1: More evidence for M2

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
Bayes factors

How convincing is the evidence that M1 is better than M2?

Moderate to strong evidence (BF > 3) to publish in psych

A posterior distribution is a conditional probability distribution that represents belief about a parameter, taking the evidence into account

Credible intervals (Highest Density Intervals)

Give us a way to express the uncertainty in estimating parameter values
Provide a range within which we believe the true value of a parameter lies, with a certain probability

With a probability of x%, the parameter lies within this interval

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
Bayesian models as psychological theory
The claim: people behave as if they do Bayesian inference.


Language: Children infer word meanings from few examples (Xu & Tenenbaum, 2007)




Perception: The brain combines noisy sensory input with prior expectations (Knill & Pouget, 2004)




Causal reasoning: People learn causal structure from sparse evidence (Griffiths & Tenenbaum, 2005)




Motor control: You catch a ball by combining visual uncertainty with learned priors (Körding & Wolpert, 2004)

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference
text:
Computing the posterior

Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampler!
Given possible priors and your data, a computer uses a Monte Carlo sampling technique to build stochastic Markov Chains, a process referred to as MCMC
We run multiple chains (e.g., 4 chains in brms) with equal numbers of iterations (e.g., 5000 iterations) in each chain to estimate convergence/stability
MCMC chains contain samples from the posterior distribution of the theory given the data

title: Introduction to Bayesian Inference

Chain of discrete events, moving forward in time

Probability of each event is a conditional probability, given the last event

Memoryless

Future events can be predicted by knowing only the current event

Issue: they can stay the same/loop

title: PSY 504: Bayes Lab 1 — From Tables to MCMC
text:
Consider the following setting: A factory produces coins, each with a different bias \(\theta_i\). You don’t know which coin you received. You have prior beliefs about which coins the factory is likely to produce — \(p(\theta_i)\). You flip the coin \(N\) times, observe \(Y\) heads, and use that data to figure out which coin you probably got — \(p(\theta_i \mid \text{data})\).
In Monday’s lecture, you saw a setting like this play out with a table of probabilities:
\[\frac{p(\text{data} = Y \mid \theta_i) \times p(\theta_i)}{\sum_i p(\text{data} = Y \mid \theta_i) \times p(\theta_i)}\]
In this lab, you’ll do all of this in R — first by hand, then with brms. The entire lab uses coins. But you’ll be using three different methods to obtain your posterior — a table, grid approximation, and MCMC.
A note on how to work through this lab: Throughout this lab, you’ll find that some code is commented out, and some is left for you to write yourself. You can uncomment the commented code to run it (CMD + Shift + C on selected lines). But before doing so, take a moment to think about how you’d write this yourself. What functions would you use? What inputs are needed, etc? Then uncomment the code, and make sure you understand each line / contrast with your approach before moving on. For the blanks marked # Your code here: that’s your turn — write the code, run it, and check that the output makes sense before continuing.

Exercise 1: Build the probability table
Use dbinom() to compute the probability of each outcome for each coin. (This is reading across a row — \(p(\text{data} \mid \theta_i)\) with \(\theta_i\) fixed.)


Code

theta_values <- c(0.2, 0.4, 0.5, 0.6, 0.8)

# For each theta_i, compute the probability of 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 heads

  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(
    probs = list(dbinom(0:5, size = 5, prob = theta))

section: Exercise 3: Compute the posterior with a flat prior
text:
Exercise 3: Compute the posterior with a flat prior
Now do what Bayes’ rule does: multiply each likelihood by a prior, then normalize so it sums to 1.
Start with a flat prior — each \(\theta_i\) is equally plausible before seeing data. You have the likelihood_table from Exercise 2. Add columns for the prior, the product of prior × likelihood, and the normalized posterior.






TipCode







Code
posterior_table <- likelihood_table %>%
  mutate(
    prior = 1 / n(),                          # flat prior: each theta_i gets equal weight
    prior_x_likelihood = prior * likelihood,   # numerator of Bayes' rule
    posterior = prior_x_likelihood / sum(prior_x_likelihood)  # normalize
  )

section: Exercise 5: Grid approximation with a flat prior
text:
Exercise 5: Grid approximation with a flat prior
Replace the 5 \(\theta_i\) values with seq(0, 1, length.out = 1000) and repeat the same multiply-and-normalize steps from Exercise 3. Then plot the posterior.






TipCode







Code
# Define a fine grid of theta values
grid <- tibble(
  theta = seq(0, 1, length.out = 1000)
) %>%
  mutate(
    prior = 1,                                           # flat prior (unnormalized is fine)
    likelihood = dbinom(3, size = 5, prob = theta),      # score each theta
    unstd_posterior = prior * likelihood,                 # prior × likelihood
    posterior = unstd_posterior / sum(unstd_posterior)     # normalize
  )

# Plot the posterior
ggplot(grid, aes(x = theta, y = posterior)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = expression(theta), y = "Posterior probability",
       title = "Posterior: 3 heads out of 5 (Y = 3, N = 5), flat prior") +
  theme_minimal()













Question 5.1

title: PSY 504: Bayes Lab 1 — From Tables to MCMC
section: Exercise 6: Grid approximation with an informative prior
text:
Exercise 6: Grid approximation with an informative prior
Now replace the flat prior with a Beta(10, 10) distribution — peaked near 0.5, skeptical of extreme values.


Code
grid_informative <- tibble(
  theta = seq(0, 1, length.out = 1000)
) %>%
  mutate(
    prior = dbeta(theta, 10, 10),                        # peaked near 0.5
    likelihood = dbinom(3, size = 5, prob = theta),
    unstd_posterior = prior * likelihood,
    posterior = unstd_posterior / sum(unstd_posterior)
  )

# Plot prior, likelihood (rescaled), and posterior together
grid_informative %>%
  mutate(
    likelihood_scaled = likelihood / max(likelihood) * max(posterior)  # rescale for visibility
  ) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = theta)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = posterior), color = "blue", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_line(aes(y = prior / sum(prior)), color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(aes(y = likelihood_scaled), color = "gray50", linetype = "dotted") +
  labs(x = expression(theta), y = "Density (rescaled)",
       title = "Blue = Posterior, Red = Prior, Gray = Likelihood") +
  theme_minimal()










Question 6.1
The posterior (blue) sits between the prior (red) and the likelihood (gray). Why? What would happen to the posterior if you had \(Y = 300\) heads out of \(N = 500\) instead of \(Y = 3\) out of \(N = 5\)?

section: Exercise 7: Watch the prior wash out
text:
Exercise 7: Watch the prior wash out
Increase the sample size while keeping the same proportion of heads (60%).


Code
# Same proportion (60% heads), increasing sample sizes
sample_sizes <- c(5, 20, 50, 200)
heads_observed <- round(0.6 * sample_sizes)  # Y = 3, 12, 30, 120

grid_by_n <- map2_dfr(sample_sizes, heads_observed, function(n, k) {
  tibble(
    theta = seq(0, 1, length.out = 1000),
    n = n,
    prior = dbeta(theta, 10, 10),
    likelihood = dbinom(k, size = n, prob = theta),
    unstd_posterior = prior * likelihood,
    posterior = unstd_posterior / sum(unstd_posterior)
  )
})

ggplot(grid_by_n, aes(x = theta, y = posterior)) +
  geom_line(color = "blue") +
  geom_line(aes(y = prior / sum(prior)), color = "red", linetype = "dashed",
            data = grid_by_n %>% filter(n == 5)) +
  facet_wrap(~ paste0("n = ", n), scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = expression(theta), y = "Posterior probability",
       title = "Same prior, more data → posterior concentrates") +
  theme_minimal()

section: Exercise 9: Fit with brms — flat prior
text:
Exercise 9: Fit with brms — flat prior
We’ll use family = binomial and a very wide prior on the intercept (which is on the logit scale). A wide prior on the logit scale approximates a flat prior on the probability scale.


Code
fit_flat <- brm(
  heads | trials(trials) ~ 1,     # intercept-only binomial model
  family = binomial(link = "logit"),
  data = coin_data,
  prior = prior(normal(0, 10), class = Intercept),  # wide prior ≈ flat on prob scale
  seed = 504,
  iter = 4000, warmup = 1000, chains = 4
)




Code
