Now model fit.

title: I Don’t Likert You: Ordinal Regression
text:
Model fit

Pseudo-\(R^2\)


r2_mcfadden(ols2)

# R2 for Generalized Linear Regression
       R2: 0.033
  adj. R2: 0.030




Not “explained variance” — but a ratio indicating how much better the model fits than an intercept-only model


McFadden’s pseudo-R-squared for ordinal regression. This is not explained variance — don’t interpret it the way you would an R-squared from OLS. It’s a ratio comparing the log-likelihood of your model to the log-likelihood of an intercept-only model. Values tend to be much lower than OLS R-squared — a McFadden’s R-squared of 0.2 to 0.4 is generally considered quite good.
Our value is quite small, which means these predictors explain only a modest amount of the variation in application intentions. That’s not unusual in social science — there are many unmeasured factors that influence a decision like this.
Let’s check our model diagnostics.

title: I Don’t Likert You: Ordinal Regression
text:
Model diagnostics

No easystats functions for ordinal models :(
sure package: surrogate residuals — based on continuous residuals

Check normality, linearity, homoscedasticity



library(sure)

set.seed(1225)

gridExtra::grid.arrange(
  autoplot.clm(ols2, nsim = 100, what = "qq"),
  autoplot.clm(ols2, nsim = 100, what = "fitted", alpha = 0.5),
  ncol = 2
)








Note


For multicollinearity, check correlations between predictor variables directly.




Unfortunately, the easystats diagnostic functions don’t work for ordinal models. The sure package fills the gap with surrogate residuals — these are simulated continuous residuals that let you do the familiar QQ plots and residual-vs-fitted plots.
J: What are surrogate residuals? They’re continuous residuals derived by mapping the ordinal outcome onto a continuous space — essentially reverse-engineering a continuous variable from your ordinal data so that standard diagnostic tools become applicable. For the Q-Q plot: all points falling on the line indicates normality is not violated. For the linearity plot: the smoothed line should be roughly flat at zero. For the box plots checking homoscedasticity: the boxes should be approximately overlapping.
The QQ plot on the left checks normality of the latent variable. If the points follow the diagonal, you’re fine. The residual-vs-fitted plot on the right checks for patterns — you want a random scatter, not a funnel or a curve.
J: For multicollinearity, you can’t use easystats directly with clm models. Instead, inspect correlations between predictors using Spearman rank correlations, which are more appropriate for ordinal and non-normal data than Pearson correlations. You can also compute VIFs from a regular linear model with the same predictors as a rough check.
Now let’s cover the formal assumptions.

title: I Don’t Likert You: Ordinal Regression
text:
Ordinal regression assumptions

Outcome is ordinal (ordered categories)
Observations are independent
Proportional odds (parallel slopes across cumulative splits)
Linearity in the log-odds (for continuous predictors)
No normality assumptions for residuals
Homogeneity of variance


Four assumptions to check, two to celebrate. First, the outcome must be ordinal — obvious, but make sure your factor levels are correctly ordered. Second, independence — no repeated measures or clustering without accounting for it. Third, proportional odds — test with Brant or a likelihood ratio test. Fourth, linearity in the log-odds for continuous predictors — check with the surrogate residual plots.
The two crossed-out lines are things you don’t need to worry about. No normality assumption for observed residuals, and no homoscedasticity requirement. Those are OLS problems that the ordinal model avoids.
One more thing before we wrap up — what if your data has clustering?

title: I Don’t Likert You: Ordinal Regression
text:
Multilevel ordinal regressions

For repeated measures or clustered/nested designs:


# Use clmm() from the ordinal package
ols_multilevel <- ordinal::clmm(
  apply ~ pared + gpa + (1 | school_id),
  data = dat
)


If you have repeated measures — say, the same person rates multiple items on a Likert scale — or nested data — students within schools — you need clmm instead of clm. The syntax is just like lmer — you add random effects in parentheses.
This is the same extension we made from glm to glmer for multilevel logistic regression. The ordinal package makes this seamless.
J: The ordinal package provides clmm(), which uses the same syntax as lme4. It is straightforward to scale up from clm to clmm for these more complex designs — you just add your random effects specification and everything else stays the same.
Now let’s close with reporting — how do you write this up?


Everything you’ve done is pointless if you can’t communicate it. Let’s talk about writing this up.

title: I Don’t Likert You: Ordinal Regression
text:
Sample write-up






Tip


A proportional odds model with a logit link (estimated using ML) was used to investigate factors influencing undergraduates’ likelihood of applying to graduate school (“unlikely,” “somewhat likely,” “very likely”). The overall model fit was modest, McFadden’s pseudo-\(R^2\) = .03. Parent education significantly predicted application likelihood, b = 1.05, z = 3.94, p < .001, OR = 2.85, 95% CI [1.55, 5.28]. Students with college-educated parents had roughly 185% higher odds of applying. Whether students attended public or private school did not significantly predict application likelihood, b = −0.06, z = −0.20, p = .844, OR = 0.94. GPA was also a significant predictor, b = 0.62, z = 2.36, p = .018, OR = 1.85. Each one-point increase in GPA was associated with 85% higher odds of applying.




Here’s a sample write-up. Notice the structure: name the model, report fit, then go predictor by predictor with log-odds, z-values, p-values, odds ratios, and CIs. Each predictor gets a plain-language interpretation after the numbers.
A few things to note: We say “proportional odds model with a logit link” — that tells readers exactly what we did. We report both the log-odds coefficient and the odds ratio with CI — give readers both metrics. And we translate the odds ratio into a percentage — “185% higher odds” is more accessible than “OR = 2.85.”
What’s missing from this write-up that you should add? The proportional odds test results, the sample size, the distribution across categories, and ideally the marginal effects.
Here’s the full checklist.

title: I Don’t Likert You: Ordinal Regression
text:
Reporting checklist

Report the model type (proportional odds / cumulative logit) and estimation method
Report log-odds coefficients and odds ratios with 95% CIs
Report thresholds (or note they are available)
Report a measure of model fit (McFadden pseudo-\(R^2\))
Test and report the proportional odds assumption (Brant test or LRT)
Consider reporting marginal effects / predicted probabilities for each category
Include sample size and distribution across response categories
Mention diagnostics (surrogate residuals, multicollinearity)


Your reporting checklist — keep this handy for your assignments and papers. The items in bold are the ones that get most often forgotten. People report the coefficients but forget to test proportional odds. They report odds ratios but not marginal effects. They don’t mention the category distribution.
Compare this to the logistic regression checklist from last time — it’s very similar, with two additions: the proportional odds test and the category distribution. The model type and fit measures are analogous.
And finally, the mistakes to avoid.

title: I Don’t Likert You: Ordinal Regression
text:
Common Mistakes

Treating ordinal data as continuous — running OLS or t-tests on Likert scales
Forgetting that coefficients are in cumulative log-odds, not probabilities
Confusing thresholds with slopes — thresholds are intercepts for each cumulative split, not effects of predictors
Ignoring the proportional odds assumption

Always test it; if it fails, consider partial proportional odds or multinomial

Interpreting odds ratios as probability ratios

OR = 3 means 3× the odds, not 3× the probability

Not visualizing predicted probabilities per category

Log-odds and ORs are hard to interpret; always plot plot_predictions()



Let me go through these one at a time. Number one: treating ordinal data as continuous. This is the most common mistake in psychology. We spent the first part of today showing you exactly why it fails — don’t do it.
Number two: forgetting the metric. Your coefficients are cumulative log-odds, not probabilities. Always convert when communicating results.
Number three: confusing thresholds and slopes. Students often look at the threshold estimates and try to interpret them as effects. They’re not — they’re properties of the measurement scale. The slopes are the effects.
Number four: not testing proportional odds. Always run the Brant test. It takes one line of code.
Number five: odds ratios are not probability ratios. OR = 3 does not mean “three times more likely.” It means three times the odds. These are different, especially when probabilities are far from 0.5.
Number six: not plotting. Ordinal regression outputs are hard to interpret from numbers alone. Always make the predicted probability plots — they’re what your audience will actually understand.
J: If you are using ordinal variables in your research, you really should be using ordinal regression. Hopefully by the end of today you’ll shift your focus from metric models toward ordinal models when working with this type of data.
That’s everything. The core message: ordinal regression is logistic regression extended to more than two ordered categories, with thresholds slicing a latent continuum. The proportional odds assumption gives you one slope per predictor. Test it, visualize it, report it properly.

    cum_odds     = cum_prop / (1 - cum_prop),

title: I Don’t Likert You: Ordinal Regression
text:
Generalized linear model
You saw this in the logistic regression lecture. Same skeleton — three components:
\[\begin{align*}
  Y_i & \sim \mathrm{Dist}(\mu_i, \tau) & \quad & \text{← Random component} \\
  g(\mu_i) & = \eta_i & \quad & \text{← Link function} \\
  \eta_i & = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{1i} + \beta_2 X_{2i} + \ldots & \quad & \text{← Linear predictor}
\end{align*}\]

Last time we filled in: Bernoulli distribution, logit link, linear predictor with one intercept and slopes.


What changes for ordinal data?

title: I Don’t Likert You: Ordinal Regression
section: Ordinal regression: Filling in the GLM
text:
Ordinal regression: Filling in the GLM
\[\begin{align*}
  Y_i & \sim \color{#d63031}{\mathrm{Cumulative}}(\pi_1, \ldots, \pi_K) & \quad & \color{#d63031}{\text{← Ordinal outcome (K ordered categories)}} \\[8pt]
  \color{#2d3436}{g(\mu_i)} & = \color{#0984e3}{\mathrm{logit}} & \quad & \color{#0984e3}{\text{← Same link as logistic regression}} \\[8pt]
  \eta_i & = \color{#00b894}{\alpha_k - (\beta_1 X_{1i} + \beta_2 X_{2i} + \ldots)} & \quad & \color{#00b894}{\text{← Thresholds + slopes}}
\end{align*}\]



Distribution
Models cumulative probability \(P(Y \leq k)\) — preserves the ordering

Link
Logit — identical to logistic regression. Nothing new here.

Linear predictor
\(K-1\) thresholds \(\alpha_k\) (one per split) + shared slopes \(\beta\) (proportional odds)

title: I Don’t Likert You: Ordinal Regression
text:
Cumulative logit model (notation)







Symbol
Meaning




\(P_k\)
Probability of being in category k


\(C_{pk}\)
Cumulative probability of being in category k or lower


1 − \(C_{pk}\)
Probability of being above category k



\[\textrm{Cumulative Odds} = \frac{P(Y \leq k)}{P(Y > k)} = \frac{C_{pk}}{1-C_{pk}}\]

Take the log to get the cumulative logit:
\[\log\left(\frac{C_{pk}}{1-C_{pk}}\right)\]








🏷️ Jargon Alert


Cumulative logit = cumulative log-odds = the same logit link you already know, just applied to cumulative probabilities.

title: I Don’t Likert You: Ordinal Regression
text:
RM: Seeing the full redistribution
A predictor doesn’t push someone into a specific category — it shifts their latent score, which redistributes probability across all categories simultaneously.

predictions(ols2, 
            newdata = datagrid(gpa = c(2.5, 3.0, 3.5, 4.0), 
                               pared = "0", public = "0")) %>%
  mutate(gpa_label = paste0("GPA = ", gpa)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = group, y = estimate, fill = group)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), width = 0.2) +
  facet_wrap(~gpa_label, nrow = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("unlikely" = color_low, 
                                "somewhat likely" = color_med, 
                                "very likely" = color_high),
                    guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Response category", y = "Predicted probability",
       title = "How probability mass redistributes as GPA increases",
       subtitle = "Non-college-educated parent, private school") +
  theme_lucid(base_size = 14) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 20, hjust = 1))









Tip


This is what the model predicts, not the raw data. As GPA rises, probability drains from “unlikely” and flows into “somewhat likely” and “very likely.” All three categories change simultaneously — that’s the ordinal redistribution.
